title: Consensus Introduction, Mechanisms and Usecases
summary: Consensus is how distributed nodes agree on one ordered log despite crashes, partitions, and lies. This guide covers what it guarantees, how quorums work, and when to pick Raft, PBFT, PoW, or PoS.
topic: Fault and Failure Tolerance + Distributed Consensus

An Overview and Comparison of Blockchain Consensus Mechanisms

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Consensus is **not voting**. It is **fault-tolerant agreement on a single ordered log** when nodes can crash, messages can be lost, and some nodes can lie. If you cannot explain why a **majority quorum** lets the system survive `f` failures and still make progress, you do not understand consensus — you just memorized acronyms.
What it is, precisely

Consensus forces `N` independent processes that share nothing but messages to behave like **one correct state machine**. Every correct node applies the **same commands in the same order** and produces the same result, even while the network drops, delays, duplicates, and reorders packets and while a minority of nodes is dead or partitioned away. The output is not a value — it is a **durable, totally ordered log** that every survivor can replay identically. That is why everything serious — configuration stores, locks, leader election, shards, ledgers — is built on top of it. The trade-off is brutal and unavoidable: you buy **consistency under faults** by paying **extra round trips and reduced availability during partitions**.

Judge every protocol by two properties and nothing else. **Safety: nothing bad ever happens** — two correct nodes never commit different values for the same log position, no committed entry is ever lost or overwritten. **Liveness: something good eventually happens** — the system keeps committing new entries as long as enough nodes can talk. Safety must hold under all asynchronous timing; liveness can only hold under partial synchrony because **deterministic consensus is impossible in a fully asynchronous network with even one crash**. That impossibility result is why every real protocol uses **timeouts, terms, and leader resignation**. It chooses to stall rather than split-brain, and that choice is the whole design.
The mechanism: propose, replicate, commit

Almost all crash-tolerant consensus uses the same shape: elect a **leader per term**, funnel all writes through it, replicate to a **quorum**, then commit. The leader appends the client command to its local log and broadcasts it. Followers persist it and acknowledge. Once a **majority** has stored it, the leader marks it committed, applies it to the state machine, and tells followers to do the same. Commitment on a majority is what makes the entry survive: any future majority — and therefore any future leader — must intersect that majority and will see it. The trade-off for this simplicity is **leader bottleneck and write latency of one to two round trips**. You get understandable correctness and fast reads from followers, you pay a single writer and cross-quorum delay on every write.

blocks.title: Crash-tolerant commit path
blocks.caption: Leader replicates to a majority before committing. No quorum, no commit.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  C[Client write] --> L[Leader appends to local log]
  L --> R[Broadcast AppendEntries to followers]
  R --> Q{Majority acked?}
  Q -->|Yes - quorum| CM[Mark entry committed]
  CM --> AP[Apply to state machine]
  AP --> RS[Respond success to client]
  Q -->|No - timeout or partition| RT[Retry in same term or step down on higher term]
  RT --> R

blocks.text: Quorum math is the mechanism, not trivia. To survive `f` crash failures you need `N = 2f+1` nodes, so a majority is `f+1`. Two majorities always overlap in at least one node, which is why a committed entry cannot be missed during leader election. Byzantine tolerance is harsher: to survive `f` actively malicious nodes you need `N = 3f+1` and quorums of `2f+1`, because lies do not cancel out — you need enough honest overlap to outvote them plus extra phases to prove it. The trade-off: **crash tolerance costs you capacity and write latency; Byzantine tolerance costs you 3x replication and quadratic messaging**. Pick crash tolerance unless participants are mutually untrusted, because you cannot afford Byzantine cost inside a single trust domain.

blocks.text: There is no best protocol, only a fault model and a latency budget. If your nodes are all yours and just crash, **Raft-style** majority replication wins on operability. If nodes can be compromised or belong to adversaries, you must pay for **Byzantine agreement** or **economic finality** with stake and slashing. If membership is open and anyone can join, you cannot use fixed quorums at all — you need **proof of resource or stake** to make Sybil attacks expensive. Name that mapping explicitly in a design review. Interviewers fail candidates who propose a blockchain where a 5-node quorum would do, or a 5-node quorum where participants do not trust each other.

blocks.text: Why each exists is more important than how. Leader-log protocols exist because **datacenter failures are crashes, not lies**, and operators need debuggability over maximal decentralization. Byzantine protocols exist because **permissioned consortia do not fully trust each other** — banks, suppliers, validators — so a leader cannot be believed without corroboration. Proof-of-work exists because **open networks cannot count members**; work makes identity expensive when you cannot whitelist. Proof-of-stake keeps that open membership but replaces energy burn with **capital at risk** to cut power cost. Authority quorums exist because sometimes you just need speed and are honest that trust is centralized. Choose by membership and adversary, not hype. Wrong fault model means either wasted money or broken safety.
How it fails in production

Consensus does not fail by returning an error. It fails by **stalling, diverging, or committing slowly** while dashboards look green. The failure mode follows directly from the safety-over-liveness choice: when a partition removes quorum, the minority stops committing to protect safety, and writes time out. When clocks drift, leases expire early and you get two leaders briefly. When disks are slow, one follower drags quorum latency and p99 explodes. When Byzantine assumptions break — more than `f` malicious — safety itself breaks and different nodes commit different histories, which is unrecoverable without human intervention. Design for the symptom, not just the algorithm.

items: **Lost quorum — writes stall, reads from leader still serve:** symptom is `write timeout` climbing while node CPU is idle. Cause is partition or two nodes down in a 5-node group. Fix is not retry storm — it is restore connectivity or expand membership via joint consensus.

**Flapping leader — no commits for seconds, term number spins:** symptom is `election timeout` logs and term counter jumping. Cause is aggressive timeouts, GC pauses, or asymmetric network. Trade-off: longer timeouts stabilize leadership but slow real failure detection.

**Slow follower drags p99 — median fine, tail awful:** symptom is quorum ack latency tracking the slowest of the fastest majority. Cause is disk fsync stall or noisy neighbor. Fix is pre-voting, parallel replication, and isolating commit path disks from compaction.

**Split-brain on stale lease reads — two clients see different values:** symptom is read-your-write violation after leader change. Cause is serving linearizable reads from leader without quorum or fencing check. Fix is quorum reads or leader lease verified by heartbeat.

**Fork that never converges — probabilistic finality violated:** symptom is two chains of similar length and reorgs deeper than your confirmation depth. Cause is high block rate relative to propagation or concentrated hash/stake power. Only fix is wait for more confirmations and cap throughput — physics, not tuning.

blocks.title: The symptom interviewers listen for
blocks.text: If writes hang but the process is healthy, say **quorum loss** first. If terms churn with no commits, say **election livelock from timeouts or partition**. Never say *the network is down* — say which side still has a majority and what it can still do. That distinction is what separates a Medium from a Junior answer.
Minimal model in code

This tiny check is the entire safety argument. A write is not durable until `can_commit` is true, and a leader is not legitimate until it has contacted a quorum that must include a holder of every committed entry. That is why followers must **persist before acking** — an ack from memory is a lie after a restart. The trade-off encoded here is durability versus latency: `fsync` before ack makes commit slower but survives power loss; ack-before-fsync is fast and wrong. In review, state it bluntly: **if you ack without durable storage, your `f` is effectively zero**.
Where it is actually used

Use consensus for **metadata, not data**. It decides who is leader, what the shard map is, whether a lock is held, whether a transaction committed — small, critical, low-throughput state where divergence is catastrophic. Then let the data plane scale without it via partitions, replicas, and eventual convergence. Real systems put configuration stores, lock services, membership, and shard coordinators behind a 3- or 5-node quorum, and keep blobs, logs, and queries out. Ledgers are the exception that proves the rule: they put data in consensus because **ordering the data is the product**, and they pay for it with single-digit to low-thousands of TPS. The trade-off: consensus gives you **one truth**; it charges you **one bottleneck**. Do not put a hot data path through it unless total order is non-negotiable.

blocks.text: How this shows up in the interview

items.title: Start from faults, not algorithms
items.text: Say: we assume crash failures, fixed 5 nodes, partial synchrony. That frames why you pick leader-log replication over Byzantine or Nakamoto. Interviewers grade this choice more than the protocol name.

items.title: Draw the write path with quorum
items.text: Walk client -> leader -> followers -> majority -> commit -> apply. State latency as 1 RTT to leader + 1 quorum RTT + fsync. Name the trade-off: linearizable writes cost quorum delay on every write.

items.title: Size the group and defend it
items.text: Argue 3 for cost, 5 for surviving 2 failures and rolling restarts. Explain why 7 is rarely worth it: higher p99 for marginal availability gain. Show f+1 and 2f+1 math without hesitation.

items.title: Handle the partition question
items.text: Minority stalls, majority keeps committing. Explain stale leader fencing with terms and why you refuse writes rather than diverge. This is the safety-over-liveness answer they want.

items.title: Extend to the use case
items.text: Place consensus only on control plane: elect shard leaders, store config, coordinate 2PC. Keep data plane partitioned. If asked about blockchains, contrast fixed-quorum finality in seconds versus probabilistic finality in minutes.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail you

items: **Consensus = majority vote on a value:** wrong. It is agreement on a log order over time, with re-elections, log repair, and re-commit. One vote never suffices because leaders change.

**More replicas always means more available:** wrong past quorum. A 7-node group is *less* available for writes than 3 if your network is flaky, because you need 4 acks instead of 2. Bigger N helps only if failures are independent.

**Proof-of-stake is just green proof-of-work:** wrong. Work ties security to ongoing energy; stake ties it to capital and slashing correctness. Failure modes differ entirely — long-range rewrites versus 51% hash rental.

**Raft is strongly consistent so reads are free:** wrong. Only leader-committed reads are linearizable, and even those need lease or quorum check. Follower reads without version are stale by design — that is the read-latency trade-off.

**Byzantine tolerance is strictly better, so use it everywhere:** wrong. It triples nodes and squares messages to survive an adversary you do not have. Inside one trust domain it is pure overhead with harder operations.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Consensus gets a fixed set of crash-prone nodes to commit one ordered log via leader replication and majority quorum, trading write latency and minority unavailability for safety; use Byzantine or stake-based variants only when nodes can lie or membership is open.**
